notes.meaning: God commands the prophet to sound an alarm with a ram's horn, warning the people that danger is near. The Assyrian army is coming swiftly like an eagle swooping down on its prey against God's people. This disaster is coming because the nation broke God's covenant, which was His sacred agreement with them, and openly rebelled against His holy law.

When trouble strikes, Israel cries out to God and claims to know Him. Their cry is insincere and comes only from a desire to escape punishment, not from genuine love or obedience. God rejects prayers that claim a close relationship while daily life denies Him.

Israel has pushed away what is good, which means they have rejected God Himself and His righteous ways. Because they treated His goodness with disgust, God will allow a fierce enemy to hunt them down. Pushing away God leaves a person completely unprotected from harm.

The northern tribes chose kings and leaders through plots and murders without asking God for guidance or approval. They also took the silver and gold God had given them and crafted idols, which directly brought about their own ruin. Relying on human politics and false gods always leads to destruction.

God utterly rejects the golden calf idol set up for the people of Samaria to worship. His anger burns against the nation because they cling stubbornly to a useless statue. He asks how long it will take before they are willing to turn away from their guilt and seek purity.

The golden calf came from human imagination and was shaped by the hands of a craftsman, so it cannot possibly be God. A created object has no power to save or help anyone in need. Because it is completely powerless, the calf idol of Samaria will be broken into pieces.

Israel's empty religious rituals and foreign alliances are like planting the wind, which will yield a harvest as violent as a whirlwind. Their efforts will fail like crops that produce no standing stalks and buds that yield no flour. Even if their fields managed to produce food, foreign invaders would quickly swallow it all up.

The nation of Israel is eaten up by invading armies and stripped of its strength. Scattered among the heathen nations, the people are treated like a cracked, worthless clay pot that nobody wants. Abandoning God turns an honored people into an object of scorn.

Israel went running to Assyria for military protection, acting like a stubborn wild donkey that wanders off alone. Instead of trusting the Lord as their faithful provider, they gave away their wealth to buy political allies, behaving like an unfaithful wife hiring lovers. Seeking help from the world rather than God only leaves a nation friendless and vulnerable.

Even though Israel pays money to win friends among foreign powers, God will gather the nation together for judgment. They will soon begin to shrink and waste away under the crushing taxes and heavy rule of the Assyrian emperor, the king of princes. Trying to purchase safety from worldly rulers only brings heavier bondage.

Ephraim built many altars throughout the land, pretending they were meant to deal with sin through sacrifices. In reality, God had commanded them to worship at only one central altar, so their extra shrines only multiplied their guilt. Inventing our own ways of worship apart from God's word turns religion into an act of sin.

God gave His people the great truths of His written law to teach them how to live rightly. Yet the Israelites treated His holy words as something strange and foreign that had nothing to do with their lives. When people turn their hearts away from the Lord, His truth begins to feel like an unwelcome stranger.

The people continued to slaughter animals as offerings and feast on the meat, but the Lord took no pleasure in their sacrifices. Outward rituals cannot hide an unrepentant heart, so God decided to call their sins to account and punish them. They would return to Egypt, meaning they would be dragged back into a state of slavery and captivity just like their ancestors once suffered.

Israel forgot the Creator who formed them into a people and busied themselves building grand palaces and idol shrines, while Judah put its trust in fortified cities with thick walls. Because both nations relied on human strength rather than their Maker, God declared He would send fire against their cities. Earthly fortresses cannot keep a nation safe when they have turned away from the living God.
